questions.question_text: A solid sphere is rolling on a horizontal plane without slipping. If the ratio of angular momentum about axis of rotation of the sphere to the total energy of moving sphere is $\pi:22$ then, the value of its angular speed will be ____________ $rad/s$ .
questions.question_html: A solid sphere is rolling on a horizontal plane without slipping. If the ratio of angular momentum about axis of rotation of the sphere to the total energy of moving sphere is $\pi:22$ then, the value of its angular speed will be ____________ $rad/s$ .
questions.explanation_text: Given that the solid sphere is rolling without slipping, we have: Angular momentum $L=(I_{\text{com}})(\omega)$ Kinetic energy $K=\frac{1}{2}(I_{\text{com}})(\omega^{2})+\frac{1}{2}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}$ For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia is $I_{\text{com}}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ , and the relationship between linear and angular velocity is $V_{\text{com}}=R\omega$ . Substituting these values into the expressions for $L$ and $K$ : $L=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}\frac{V_{\text{com}}}{R}=\frac{2MRV_{\text{com}}}{5}$ $K=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{5}MR^{2})\frac{V_{\text{com}}^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}=\frac{7}{10}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}$ Now, the given ratio of $\frac{L}{K}$ is $\frac{\pi}{22}$ : $\frac{L}{K}=\frac{4}{7}\frac{R}{V_{\text{com}}}=\frac{\pi}{22}$ Since $V_{\text{com}}=R\omega$ , we can substitute this relationship into the equation and solve for $\omega$ : $\frac{4}{7}\frac{R}{R\omega}=\frac{\pi}{22}$ $\frac{4}{7\omega}=\frac{\pi}{22}$ $\omega=\frac{4}{7} \times \frac{22}{\pi} \times 7=4$ Thus, the value of the angular speed is $4\text{rad/s}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given that the solid sphere is rolling without slipping, we have:

Angular momentum $L=(I_{\text{com}})(\omega)$

Kinetic energy $K=\frac{1}{2}(I_{\text{com}})(\omega^{2})+\frac{1}{2}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia is $I_{\text{com}}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ , and the relationship between linear and angular velocity is $V_{\text{com}}=R\omega$ .

Substituting these values into the expressions for $L$ and $K$ :

$L=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}\frac{V_{\text{com}}}{R}=\frac{2MRV_{\text{com}}}{5}$

$K=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{5}MR^{2})\frac{V_{\text{com}}^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}=\frac{7}{10}MV_{\text{com}}^{2}$

Now, the given ratio of $\frac{L}{K}$ is $\frac{\pi}{22}$ :

$\frac{L}{K}=\frac{4}{7}\frac{R}{V_{\text{com}}}=\frac{\pi}{22}$

Since $V_{\text{com}}=R\omega$ , we can substitute this relationship into the equation and solve for $\omega$ :

$\frac{4}{7}\frac{R}{R\omega}=\frac{\pi}{22}$

$\frac{4}{7\omega}=\frac{\pi}{22}$

$\omega=\frac{4}{7} \times \frac{22}{\pi} \times 7=4$

Thus, the value of the angular speed is $4\text{rad/s}$ .

questions.question_text: A force of $-P\hat{k}$ acts on the origin of the coordinate system. The torque about the point $(2,-3)$ is $P(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j})$ , The ratio of $\frac{a}{b}$ is $\frac{x}{2}$ . The value of $x$ is -
questions.question_html: A force of $-P\hat{k}$ acts on the origin of the coordinate system. The torque about the point $(2,-3)$ is $P(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j})$ , The ratio of $\frac{a}{b}$ is $\frac{x}{2}$ . The value of $x$ is -
questions.explanation_text: Let the point where the force acts be A, the origin of the coordinate system (0, 0, 0), and let the point about which the torque is calculated be B (2, -3, 0). The force vector is given by $\vec{F}=-P\hat{k}$ . To find the torque, we first find the position vector of point A with respect to point B: $\vec{r}_{AB}=\vec{r}_{A}-\vec{r}_{B}=(0-2)\hat{i}+(0-(-3))\hat{j}+(0-0)\hat{k}=-2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$ To calculate the cross product, we can use the determinant method with a 3x3 matrix: $\vec{\tau}=\vec{r}_{AB} \times \vec{F}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -P \end{aligned}|$ Now, we will calculate the cross product components by expanding the determinant along the first row: 1. $\tau_{i}=\hat{i}|\begin{aligned} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -P \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}((3)(-P)-(0)(0))=-3P\hat{i}$ 2. $\tau_{j}=-\hat{j}|\begin{aligned} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -P \end{aligned}|=-\hat{j}((-2)(-P)-(0)(0))=-2P\hat{j}$ (Notice the negative sign in front of the $\hat{j}$ term, as it comes from the expansion of the determinant.) 3. $\tau_{k}=\hat{k}|\begin{aligned} -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{aligned}|=\hat{k}((-2)(0)-(3)(0))=0\hat{k}$ Now, combine the components to get the torque vector: $\vec{\tau}=-3P\hat{i}-2P\hat{j}+0\hat{k}=-3P\hat{i}-2P\hat{j}$ Comparing this to the given torque vector $\vec{\tau}=P(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j})$ , we find that: $a=-3$ $b=-2$ Thus, the ratio $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-3}{-2}=\frac{x}{2}$ . Therefore, $x=3$ .

questions.question_text: Two identical solid spheres each of mass $2kg$ and radii $10cm$ are fixed at the ends of a light rod. The separation between the centres of the spheres is $40cm$ . The moment of inertia of the system about an axis perpendicular to the rod passing through its middle point is __________ $\times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$
questions.question_html: Two identical solid spheres each of mass $2kg$ and radii $10cm$ are fixed at the ends of a light rod. The separation between the centres of the spheres is $40cm$ . The moment of inertia of the system about an axis perpendicular to the rod passing through its middle point is __________ $\times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$
questions.explanation_text: The problem requires calculating the moment of inertia of the system consisting of two identical solid spheres fixed at the ends of a light rod. We need to find the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the rod and passing through its midpoint. First, let’s identify the moment of inertia of each solid sphere about its own center, which is given by the formula: $I_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{2}{5}mr^{2}$ Where: $m$ is the mass of the sphere = $2kg$ $r$ is the radius of the sphere = $0.1m$ Substituting the values: $I_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{2}{5} \times 2kg \times (0.1m)^{2}=\frac{4}{5} \times 0.01kgm^{2}=0.008kgm^{2}$ Now, we need the moment of inertia of the two spheres about the axis passing through the midpoint of the rod. This requires using the parallel axis theorem, which states: $I_{\text{total}}=I_{\text{sphere}}+md^{2}$ Where: $d$ is the distance from the center of the sphere to the axis through the rod’s midpoint = $0.2m$ Calculating the additional inertia due to the parallel axis theorem for one sphere: $I_{\text{parallel}}=md^{2}=2kg \times (0.2m)^{2}=2kg \times 0.04m^{2}=0.08kgm^{2}$ The total moment of inertia for one sphere about the midpoint of the rod is: $I_{\text{one sphere, total}}=I_{\text{sphere}}+I_{\text{parallel}}=0.008kgm^{2}+0.08kgm^{2}=0.088kgm^{2}$ Since there are two identical spheres, the total moment of inertia of the system is: $I_{\text{system}}=2 \times 0.088kgm^{2}=0.176kgm^{2}$ Converting the result to the given form: $0.176kgm^{2}=176 \times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$ So, the moment of inertia of the system about the given axis is: $176 \times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
The problem requires calculating the moment of inertia of the system consisting of two identical solid spheres fixed at the ends of a light rod. We need to find the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the rod and passing through its midpoint.

First, let’s identify the moment of inertia of each solid sphere about its own center, which is given by the formula:

$I_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{2}{5}mr^{2}$

Where:

  • $m$ is the mass of the sphere = $2kg$
  • $r$ is the radius of the sphere = $0.1m$

Substituting the values:

$I_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{2}{5} \times 2kg \times (0.1m)^{2}=\frac{4}{5} \times 0.01kgm^{2}=0.008kgm^{2}$

Now, we need the moment of inertia of the two spheres about the axis passing through the midpoint of the rod. This requires using the parallel axis theorem, which states:

$I_{\text{total}}=I_{\text{sphere}}+md^{2}$

Where:

  • $d$ is the distance from the center of the sphere to the axis through the rod’s midpoint = $0.2m$

Calculating the additional inertia due to the parallel axis theorem for one sphere:

$I_{\text{parallel}}=md^{2}=2kg \times (0.2m)^{2}=2kg \times 0.04m^{2}=0.08kgm^{2}$

The total moment of inertia for one sphere about the midpoint of the rod is:

$I_{\text{one sphere, total}}=I_{\text{sphere}}+I_{\text{parallel}}=0.008kgm^{2}+0.08kgm^{2}=0.088kgm^{2}$

Since there are two identical spheres, the total moment of inertia of the system is:

$I_{\text{system}}=2 \times 0.088kgm^{2}=0.176kgm^{2}$

Converting the result to the given form:

$0.176kgm^{2}=176 \times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$

So, the moment of inertia of the system about the given axis is:

$176 \times 10^{-3}kgm^{2}$

questions.question_text: For a rolling spherical shell, the ratio of rotational kinetic energy and total kinetic energy is $\frac{x}{5}$ . The value of $x$ is ___________.
questions.question_html: For a rolling spherical shell, the ratio of rotational kinetic energy and total kinetic energy is $\frac{x}{5}$ . The value of $x$ is ___________.
questions.explanation_text: For a rolling spherical shell, we must consider the fact that it has both translational and rotational kinetic energy. The total kinetic energy ( $K_{total}$ ) can be expressed as the sum of the translational kinetic energy ( $K_{trans}$ ) and the rotational kinetic energy ( $K_{rot}$ ): $K_{total}=K_{trans}+K_{rot}$ The translational kinetic energy of an object with mass (m) and linear velocity (v) is given by: $K_{trans}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ The rotational kinetic energy of a rolling spherical shell with moment of inertia (I) and angular velocity (ω) is given by: $K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ For a rolling object without slipping, the relationship between linear velocity (v) and angular velocity (ω) is: $v=R\omega$ Where R is the radius of the spherical shell. The moment of inertia for a spherical shell is given by: $I=\frac{2}{3}mR^{2}$ Now, we can substitute the moment of inertia and the relationship between linear and angular velocity into the equation for rotational kinetic energy: $K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3}mR^{2})(\frac{v}{R})^{2}$ Simplifying the equation: $K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3}mR^{2})\frac{v^{2}}{R^{2}}$ $K_{rot}=\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}$ Now, we can find the ratio of rotational kinetic energy to total kinetic energy: $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}}$ Simplifying the equation: $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{5}{6}}$ Multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 6: $\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{2}{5}$ Comparing this to the given ratio of $\frac{x}{5}$ , we can determine that the value of $x$ is 2.
questions.explanation_html:
For a rolling spherical shell, we must consider the fact that it has both translational and rotational kinetic energy. The total kinetic energy ( $K_{total}$ ) can be expressed as the sum of the translational kinetic energy ( $K_{trans}$ ) and the rotational kinetic energy ( $K_{rot}$ ):

$K_{total}=K_{trans}+K_{rot}$

The translational kinetic energy of an object with mass (m) and linear velocity (v) is given by:

$K_{trans}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

The rotational kinetic energy of a rolling spherical shell with moment of inertia (I) and angular velocity (ω) is given by:

$K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$

For a rolling object without slipping, the relationship between linear velocity (v) and angular velocity (ω) is:

$v=R\omega$

Where R is the radius of the spherical shell.

The moment of inertia for a spherical shell is given by:

$I=\frac{2}{3}mR^{2}$

Now, we can substitute the moment of inertia and the relationship between linear and angular velocity into the equation for rotational kinetic energy:

$K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3}mR^{2})(\frac{v}{R})^{2}$

Simplifying the equation:

$K_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3}mR^{2})\frac{v^{2}}{R^{2}}$

$K_{rot}=\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}$

Now, we can find the ratio of rotational kinetic energy to total kinetic energy:

$\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{3}mv^{2}}$

Simplifying the equation:

$\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{5}{6}}$

Multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 6:

$\frac{K_{rot}}{K_{total}}=\frac{2}{5}$

Comparing this to the given ratio of $\frac{x}{5}$ , we can determine that the value of $x$ is 2.

Energy remains conserve during whole journey.

$K_{\cdot}E_{i}+P.E_{\cdot i}=K_{\cdot}E_{f}+P.E_{\cdot f}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{5}{2}mv^{2}=mgH( \because K.E._{f}=0) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow H=\frac{5}{6} \times \frac{v^{2}}{g} \\ \\ & =\frac{5 \times (3)^{2}}{6 \times 10} \\ \\ & =\frac{15}{20}m=0.75m=75cm \end{aligned}$

It starts off with a purely sliding motion at $t=0s$ . After $2s$ it acquires a purely rolling motion (see figure). The total kinetic energy of the disc after $2s$ will be __________ $J$ (given, coefficient of friction is $0.3$ and $g=10m/s^{2}$ ).
questions.question_html: A uniform disc of mass $0.5kg$ and radius $r$ is projected with velocity $18m/s$ at $t=0$ s on a rough horizontal surface. It starts off with a purely sliding motion at $t=0s$ . After $2s$ it acquires a purely rolling motion (see figure). The total kinetic energy of the disc after $2s$ will be __________ $J$ (given, coefficient of friction is $0.3$ and $g=10m/s^{2}$ ).
questions.explanation_text: $v=v_{0}-\mu gt$ $\Rightarrow v=18-0.3 \times 10 \times 2=12$ m/s $\Rightarrow$ Kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mv^{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{3}{4}mv^{2}=\frac{3}{4} \times 0.5 \times 144J=54J$
questions.explanation_html:
$v=v_{0}-\mu gt$

$\Rightarrow v=18-0.3 \times 10 \times 2=12$ m/s

$\Rightarrow$ Kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{mv^{2}}{2}$

$=\frac{3}{4}mv^{2}=\frac{3}{4} \times 0.5 \times 144J=54J$

questions.question_text: If a solid sphere of mass 5 kg and a disc of mass 4 kg have the same radius. Then the ratio of moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane to the moment of inertia of the sphere about its tangent will be $\frac{x}{7}$ . The value of $x$ is ___________.
questions.question_html: If a solid sphere of mass 5 kg and a disc of mass 4 kg have the same radius. Then the ratio of moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane to the moment of inertia of the sphere about its tangent will be $\frac{x}{7}$ . The value of $x$ is ___________.
questions.explanation_text:
Solid Sphere : $\begin{aligned} & I_{\text{tangent}}=I_{cm}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{2}{5}mR^{2}+mR^{2}=\frac{7}{5}mR^{2} \\ \\ & =7R^{2}(m=5kg) \end{aligned}$ CIRCULAR DISC : $\begin{aligned} I_{\text{disc}} & =I_{cm}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{mR^{2}}{4}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{5}{4}mR^{2} \\ \\ & =5R^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\frac{l_{\text{disc}}}{l_{\text{tangent}}}=\frac{5}{7}$ Concept : 1. For Solid Sphere : Position of the axis of rotation : About its diametric
 axis which passes
through its centre
of mass Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ Radius of gyration (K) = $\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R$ Position of the axis of rotation : About a tangent to
the sphere Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{7}{5}MR^{2}$ Radius of gyration (K) = $\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}R$ 2. For CIRCULAR DISC : Position of the axis of rotation : About an axis perpendicular to the plane and passes through the centre Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ Radius of gyration (K) = $\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$ Position of the axis of rotation : About the diametric axis Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{1}{4}MR^{2}$ Radius of gyration (K) = $\frac{R}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Solid Sphere :

$\begin{aligned} & I_{\text{tangent}}=I_{cm}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{2}{5}mR^{2}+mR^{2}=\frac{7}{5}mR^{2} \\ \\ & =7R^{2}(m=5kg) \end{aligned}$



CIRCULAR DISC :

$\begin{aligned} I_{\text{disc}} & =I_{cm}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{mR^{2}}{4}+mR^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{5}{4}mR^{2} \\ \\ & =5R^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\frac{l_{\text{disc}}}{l_{\text{tangent}}}=\frac{5}{7}$



Concept :

1. For Solid Sphere :

Position of the axis of rotation : About its diametric axis which passes through its centre of mass


Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$

Radius of gyration (K) = $\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R$

Position of the axis of rotation : About a tangent to the sphere


Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{7}{5}MR^{2}$

Radius of gyration (K) = $\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}R$



2. For CIRCULAR DISC :

Position of the axis of rotation : About an axis perpendicular to the plane and passes through the centre


Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$

Radius of gyration (K) = $\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

Position of the axis of rotation : About the diametric axis


Moment of Inertia (I) = $\frac{1}{4}MR^{2}$

Radius of gyration (K) = $\frac{R}{2}$

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A solid sphere and a solid cylinder of same mass and radius are rolling on a horizontal surface without slipping. The ratio of their radius of gyrations respectively $(k_{\text{sph}}:k_{\text{cyl}})$ is $2:\sqrt{x}$ . The value of $x$ is ____________ .
questions.question_html: A solid sphere and a solid cylinder of same mass and radius are rolling on a horizontal surface without slipping. The ratio of their radius of gyrations respectively $(k_{\text{sph}}:k_{\text{cyl}})$ is $2:\sqrt{x}$ . The value of $x$ is ____________ .
questions.explanation_text: Let the mass of both the solid sphere and the solid cylinder be $M$ , and let their common radius be $R$ . The moment of inertia $I$ of a solid sphere and a solid cylinder are given by: $I_{spℎ}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ $I_{cyl}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ The radius of gyration $k$ is related to the moment of inertia $I$ by the formula $I=Mk^{2}$ . Therefore, we can find the radius of gyration for both the solid sphere and the solid cylinder using their respective moments of inertia: $k_{spℎ}^{2}=\frac{I_{spℎ}}{M}=\frac{2}{5}R^{2}$ $k_{cyl}^{2}=\frac{I_{cyl}}{M}=\frac{1}{2}R^{2}$ Now, let's find the ratio of their radius of gyrations: $\frac{k_{spℎ}}{k_{cyl}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$ Squaring both sides: $\frac{k_{spℎ}^{2}}{k_{cyl}^{2}}=\frac{4}{x}$ Substituting the expressions for $k_{spℎ}^{2}$ and $k_{cyl}^{2}$ : $\frac{\frac{2}{5}R^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}R^{2}}=\frac{4}{x}$ Simplifying and solving for $x$ : $\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{2}{1}=\frac{4}{x}$ $\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4}{x}$ Thus, $x=5$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Let the mass of both the solid sphere and the solid cylinder be $M$ , and let their common radius be $R$ . The moment of inertia $I$ of a solid sphere and a solid cylinder are given by:

$I_{spℎ}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$

$I_{cyl}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$

The radius of gyration $k$ is related to the moment of inertia $I$ by the formula $I=Mk^{2}$ . Therefore, we can find the radius of gyration for both the solid sphere and the solid cylinder using their respective moments of inertia:

$k_{spℎ}^{2}=\frac{I_{spℎ}}{M}=\frac{2}{5}R^{2}$

$k_{cyl}^{2}=\frac{I_{cyl}}{M}=\frac{1}{2}R^{2}$

Now, let's find the ratio of their radius of gyrations:

$\frac{k_{spℎ}}{k_{cyl}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$

Squaring both sides:

$\frac{k_{spℎ}^{2}}{k_{cyl}^{2}}=\frac{4}{x}$

Substituting the expressions for $k_{spℎ}^{2}$ and $k_{cyl}^{2}$ :

$\frac{\frac{2}{5}R^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}R^{2}}=\frac{4}{x}$

Simplifying and solving for $x$ :

$\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{2}{1}=\frac{4}{x}$

$\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4}{x}$

Thus, $x=5$ .

questions.question_text: A circular plate is rotating in horizontal plane, about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to the plate, with an angular velocity $\omega$ . A person sits at the center having two dumbbells in his hands. When he stretches out his hands, the moment of inertia of the system becomes triple. If E be the initial Kinetic energy of the system, then final Kinetic energy will be $\frac{E}{x}$ . The value of $x$ is
questions.question_html: A circular plate is rotating in horizontal plane, about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to the plate, with an angular velocity $\omega$ . A person sits at the center having two dumbbells in his hands. When he stretches out his hands, the moment of inertia of the system becomes triple. If E be the initial Kinetic energy of the system, then final Kinetic energy will be $\frac{E}{x}$ . The value of $x$ is
questions.explanation_text: The conservation of angular momentum states that the angular momentum (L) remains constant. The relation between kinetic energy (KE), angular momentum (L), and moment of inertia (I) is given by: $KE=\frac{L^{2}}{2I}$ Using this relation, we can find the ratio of the final kinetic energy ( $KE_{\text{final}}$ ) to the initial kinetic energy ( $KE_{\text{initial}}$ or E): $\frac{KE_{\text{final}}}{KE_{\text{initial}}}=\frac{I_{\text{initial}}}{I_{\text{final}}}$ Since the moment of inertia triples, we have $I_{\text{final}}=3I_{\text{initial}}$ . Therefore, $\frac{KE_{\text{final}}}{E}=\frac{I_{\text{initial}}}{3I_{\text{initial}}}=\frac{1}{3}$ This means that the final kinetic energy of the system is: $KE_{\text{final}}=\frac{E}{3}$ So, the value of $x$ is 3.
questions.explanation_html:
The conservation of angular momentum states that the angular momentum (L) remains constant. The relation between kinetic energy (KE), angular momentum (L), and moment of inertia (I) is given by:

$KE=\frac{L^{2}}{2I}$

Using this relation, we can find the ratio of the final kinetic energy ( $KE_{\text{final}}$ ) to the initial kinetic energy ( $KE_{\text{initial}}$ or E):

$\frac{KE_{\text{final}}}{KE_{\text{initial}}}=\frac{I_{\text{initial}}}{I_{\text{final}}}$

Since the moment of inertia triples, we have $I_{\text{final}}=3I_{\text{initial}}$ . Therefore,

$\frac{KE_{\text{final}}}{E}=\frac{I_{\text{initial}}}{3I_{\text{initial}}}=\frac{1}{3}$

This means that the final kinetic energy of the system is:

$KE_{\text{final}}=\frac{E}{3}$

So, the value of $x$ is 3.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: The moment of inertia of a semicircular ring about an axis, passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane of ring, is $\frac{1}{x}MR^{2}$ , where $R$ is the radius and $M$ is the mass of the semicircular ring. The value of $x$ will be __________.
questions.question_html: The moment of inertia of a semicircular ring about an axis, passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane of ring, is $\frac{1}{x}MR^{2}$ , where $R$ is the radius and $M$ is the mass of the semicircular ring. The value of $x$ will be __________.
questions.explanation_text: To solve this problem, we need to understand the concept of moment of inertia. Moment of inertia is a measure of an object's resistance to rotational motion. It depends on the mass distribution of the object and the axis of rotation. For a continuous object like a semicircular ring, we can calculate the moment of inertia by integrating over the entire object. Here's how we can approach this problem: 1. Divide the semicircular ring into small mass elements: Imagine the semicircular ring divided into infinitesimally small mass elements, each with mass $dm$ . 2. Calculate the moment of inertia of each element: The moment of inertia of each element about the axis passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane of the ring is given by $dI=dmR^{2}$ , where R is the radius of the ring. 3. Integrate to find the total moment of inertia: To find the total moment of inertia, we need to integrate $dI$ over the entire ring. This means integrating from $0$ to $\pi$ (the angle spanned by the semicircle) with respect to the angle $\theta$ . 4. Relate $dm$ to the total mass: Since the ring has a uniform mass distribution, we can express the mass of each element $dm$ as a fraction of the total mass $M$ : $dm=\frac{M}{\pi R}Rd\theta=\frac{M}{\pi}d\theta$ . Now, let's perform the integration: $I=\int_{0}^{\pi}dI=\int_{0}^{\pi}dmR^{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{M}{\pi}d\theta R^{2}$ $I=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}[\theta]_{0}^{\pi}$ $I=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}[\pi-0]=MR^{2}$ Therefore, the moment of inertia of the semicircular ring about the given axis is $MR^{2}$ . Comparing this to the given formula, we find that $x=1$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To solve this problem, we need to understand the concept of moment of inertia. Moment of inertia is a measure of an object's resistance to rotational motion. It depends on the mass distribution of the object and the axis of rotation.

For a continuous object like a semicircular ring, we can calculate the moment of inertia by integrating over the entire object. Here's how we can approach this problem:

1. Divide the semicircular ring into small mass elements: Imagine the semicircular ring divided into infinitesimally small mass elements, each with mass $dm$ .

2. Calculate the moment of inertia of each element: The moment of inertia of each element about the axis passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane of the ring is given by $dI=dmR^{2}$ , where R is the radius of the ring.

3. Integrate to find the total moment of inertia: To find the total moment of inertia, we need to integrate $dI$ over the entire ring. This means integrating from $0$ to $\pi$ (the angle spanned by the semicircle) with respect to the angle $\theta$ .

4. Relate $dm$ to the total mass: Since the ring has a uniform mass distribution, we can express the mass of each element $dm$ as a fraction of the total mass $M$ : $dm=\frac{M}{\pi R}Rd\theta=\frac{M}{\pi}d\theta$ .

Now, let's perform the integration:

$I=\int_{0}^{\pi}dI=\int_{0}^{\pi}dmR^{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{M}{\pi}d\theta R^{2}$

$I=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}[\theta]_{0}^{\pi}$

$I=\frac{MR^{2}}{\pi}[\pi-0]=MR^{2}$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the semicircular ring about the given axis is $MR^{2}$ . Comparing this to the given formula, we find that $x=1$ .

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A light rope is wound around a hollow cylinder of mass 5 kg and radius 70 cm. The rope is pulled with a force of 52.5 N. The angular acceleration of the cylinder will be _________ rad s $^{-2}$ .
questions.question_html: A light rope is wound around a hollow cylinder of mass 5 kg and radius 70 cm. The rope is pulled with a force of 52.5 N. The angular acceleration of the cylinder will be _________ rad s $^{-2}$ .
questions.explanation_text: In this problem, the net force on the cylinder is the tension $T$ in the rope, which is equal to the force applied to the rope: $F=T=52.5N$ The force causes the cylinder to accelerate with an angular acceleration $\alpha$ , which is related to its linear acceleration $a$ and the radius of the cylinder $R$ by the equation: $\alpha=\frac{a}{R}$ The linear acceleration $a$ of the cylinder can be found using the formula $F=ma$ : $ma=F=52.5N$ where $m=5kg$ is the mass of the cylinder. Solving for $a$ , we get: $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{52.5N}{5kg}=10.5m/s^{2}$ Substituting this value of $a$ into the equation for $\alpha$ , we get: $\alpha=\frac{a}{R}=\frac{10.5m/s^{2}}{0.7m}=15rad/s^{2}$ Therefore, the angular acceleration of the cylinder is $15rad/s^{2}$ . Alternate Method: Let's first draw a free body diagram of the cylinder. The force $F$ applied to the rope creates a tension in the rope, which in turn exerts a force on the cylinder in the opposite direction. This force is given by: $T=F$ where $T$ is the tension in the rope. The cylinder also experiences a torque due to the tension in the rope, which causes it to rotate. The torque is given by: $\tau=TR$ where $R$ is the radius of the cylinder. The net torque on the cylinder is equal to the product of the moment of inertia $I$ of the cylinder and its angular acceleration $\alpha$ : $\tau=I\alpha$ The moment of inertia of a hollow cylinder about its geometrical axis which is parallel to its length is given by: $I=MR^{2}$ where $M$ is the mass of the cylinder. Substituting the given values, we get: $\tau=TR=I\alpha=MR^{2}\alpha$ Solving for $\alpha$ , we get: $\alpha=\frac{T}{MR}=\frac{F}{MR}=\frac{52.5N}{5kg \cdot 0.7m}=15rad/s^{2}$ Therefore, the angular acceleration of the cylinder is $15rad/s^{2}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
In this problem, the net force on the cylinder is the tension $T$ in the rope, which is equal to the force applied to the rope:

$F=T=52.5N$

The force causes the cylinder to accelerate with an angular acceleration $\alpha$ , which is related to its linear acceleration $a$ and the radius of the cylinder $R$ by the equation:

$\alpha=\frac{a}{R}$

The linear acceleration $a$ of the cylinder can be found using the formula $F=ma$ :

$ma=F=52.5N$

where $m=5kg$ is the mass of the cylinder. Solving for $a$ , we get:

$a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{52.5N}{5kg}=10.5m/s^{2}$

Substituting this value of $a$ into the equation for $\alpha$ , we get:

$\alpha=\frac{a}{R}=\frac{10.5m/s^{2}}{0.7m}=15rad/s^{2}$

Therefore, the angular acceleration of the cylinder is $15rad/s^{2}$ .

Alternate Method:

Let's first draw a free body diagram of the cylinder. The force $F$ applied to the rope creates a tension in the rope, which in turn exerts a force on the cylinder in the opposite direction. This force is given by:

$T=F$

where $T$ is the tension in the rope. The cylinder also experiences a torque due to the tension in the rope, which causes it to rotate. The torque is given by:

$\tau=TR$

where $R$ is the radius of the cylinder.

The net torque on the cylinder is equal to the product of the moment of inertia $I$ of the cylinder and its angular acceleration $\alpha$ :

$\tau=I\alpha$

The moment of inertia of a hollow cylinder about its geometrical axis which is parallel to its length is given by:

$I=MR^{2}$

where $M$ is the mass of the cylinder.

Substituting the given values, we get:

$\tau=TR=I\alpha=MR^{2}\alpha$

Solving for $\alpha$ , we get:

$\alpha=\frac{T}{MR}=\frac{F}{MR}=\frac{52.5N}{5kg \cdot 0.7m}=15rad/s^{2}$

Therefore, the angular acceleration of the cylinder is $15rad/s^{2}$ .

questions.explanation_text: Given that the radii of gyration for the ring and the solid sphere are equal, we have: $K_{1}=K_{2}$ For the ring, the moment of inertia is: $I_{ring}=mR_{1}^{2}=mK_{1}^{2}$ Thus, the radius of gyration for the ring is: $K_{1}=R_{1}$ For the solid sphere, the moment of inertia is: $I_{spℎere}=\frac{2}{5}m^{'}R_{2}^{2}=m^{'}K_{2}^{2}$ Hence, the radius of gyration for the solid sphere is: $K_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R_{2}$ Since the radii of gyration are equal: $R_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R_{2}$ Therefore, the ratio of the radius of the ring to that of the sphere is: $\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$ So, the value of $x$ is: $x=5$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that the radii of gyration for the ring and the solid sphere are equal, we have:

$K_{1}=K_{2}$

For the ring, the moment of inertia is:

$I_{ring}=mR_{1}^{2}=mK_{1}^{2}$

Thus, the radius of gyration for the ring is:

$K_{1}=R_{1}$

For the solid sphere, the moment of inertia is:

$I_{spℎere}=\frac{2}{5}m^{'}R_{2}^{2}=m^{'}K_{2}^{2}$

Hence, the radius of gyration for the solid sphere is:

$K_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R_{2}$

Since the radii of gyration are equal:

$R_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R_{2}$

Therefore, the ratio of the radius of the ring to that of the sphere is:

$\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$

So, the value of $x$ is:

$x=5$

questions.question_text: A solid cylinder length is suspended symmetrically through two massless strings, as shown in the figure. The distance from the initial rest position, the cylinder should be unbinding the strings to achieve a speed of $4ms^{-1}$ , is ____________ cm. (take g = $10ms^{-2}$ )
questions.question_html: A solid cylinder length is suspended symmetrically through two massless strings, as shown in the figure. The distance from the initial rest position, the cylinder should be unbinding the strings to achieve a speed of $4ms^{-1}$ , is ____________ cm. (take g = $10ms^{-2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: In case of rotational motion of a rigid body like this, the kinetic energy is not just due to the linear motion, but also due to its rotation. For a solid cylinder, the moment of inertia I is given by $\frac{1}{2}mr^{2}$ . The kinetic energy due to rotation is given by $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ . But we also know that $\omega=\frac{v}{r}$ , hence the rotational kinetic energy can be written as $\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{1}{4}mv^{2}$ , where $\frac{1}{2}$ is from the moment of inertia of the solid cylinder. Therefore, the total kinetic energy (linear + rotational) when the string snaps is $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{4}mv^{2}=\frac{3}{4}mv^{2}$ . Equating this to the potential energy $mgℎ$ and solving for h gives the result : $ℎ=\frac{v^{2}}{2g} \times \frac{3}{2}=1.2m=120cm$ Alternate Method : Applying COE, we get $mgℎ=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}(1+\frac{K^{2}}{r^{2}})$ $K=$ radius of gyration For a solid cylinder, $\frac{K^{2}}{r^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\begin{aligned} \therefore ℎ & =\frac{v^{2}}{2g}(1+\frac{1}{2}) \\ \\ & =\frac{16}{2 \times 10} \times \frac{3}{2} \\ \\ & =1.2m \\ \\ & =120cm \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
In case of rotational motion of a rigid body like this, the kinetic energy is not just due to the linear motion, but also due to its rotation.

For a solid cylinder, the moment of inertia I is given by $\frac{1}{2}mr^{2}$ . The kinetic energy due to rotation is given by $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ . But we also know that $\omega=\frac{v}{r}$ , hence the rotational kinetic energy can be written as $\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{1}{4}mv^{2}$ , where $\frac{1}{2}$ is from the moment of inertia of the solid cylinder.

Therefore, the total kinetic energy (linear + rotational) when the string snaps is $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{1}{4}mv^{2}=\frac{3}{4}mv^{2}$ .

Equating this to the potential energy $mgℎ$ and solving for h gives the result :

$ℎ=\frac{v^{2}}{2g} \times \frac{3}{2}=1.2m=120cm$

Alternate Method :

Applying COE, we get

$mgℎ=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}(1+\frac{K^{2}}{r^{2}})$

$K=$ radius of gyration

For a solid cylinder, $\frac{K^{2}}{r^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} \therefore ℎ & =\frac{v^{2}}{2g}(1+\frac{1}{2}) \\ \\ & =\frac{16}{2 \times 10} \times \frac{3}{2} \\ \\ & =1.2m \\ \\ & =120cm \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: A 2 kg steel rod of length 0.6 m is clamped on a table vertically at its lower end and is free to rotate in vertical plane. questions.explanation_text: by energy conservation $mgl=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{ml^{2}\omega^{2}}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \omega=\sqrt{\frac{6g}{l}}$ As we know the relation between the linear speed and angular speed, $v=\omega r=\omega l=\sqrt{6gl}$ $v=\sqrt{6 \times 10 \times .6}$ = 6 m/s Hence, the speed of the free end of the rod when it passes through its lowest position is 6 m/s.
questions.explanation_html:
by energy conservation $mgl=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{ml^{2}\omega^{2}}{3}$

$\Rightarrow \omega=\sqrt{\frac{6g}{l}}$

As we know the relation between the linear speed and angular speed,

$v=\omega r=\omega l=\sqrt{6gl}$

$v=\sqrt{6 \times 10 \times .6}$ = 6 m/s

Hence, the speed of the free end of the rod when it passes through its lowest position is 6 m/s.

questions.question_text: A particle of mass 'm' is moving in time 't' on a trajectory given by $\vec{r}=10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}$ Where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are dimensional constants. The angular momentum of the particle becomes the same as it was for t = 0 at time t = ____________ seconds.
questions.question_html:
A particle of mass 'm' is moving in time 't' on a trajectory given by

$\vec{r}=10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}$

Where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are dimensional constants.

The angular momentum of the particle becomes the same as it was for t = 0 at time t = ____________ seconds.
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{r}=10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}$ $\vec{v}=20\alpha t\hat{i}+5\beta\hat{j}$ $\vec{L}=m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$ $=m[10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}] \times [20\alpha t\hat{i}+5\beta\hat{j}]$ $\vec{L}=m[50\alpha\beta t^{2}\hat{k}-10\alpha\beta(t^{2}-5t)\hat{k}]$ At t = 0, $\vec{L}=\vec{0}$ $50\alpha\beta t^{2}-100\alpha\beta(t^{2}-5t)=0$ t $-$ 2 (t $-$ 5) = 0 t = 10 sec
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{r}=10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}$

$\vec{v}=20\alpha t\hat{i}+5\beta\hat{j}$

$\vec{L}=m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$

$=m[10\alpha t^{2}\hat{i}+5\beta(t-5)\hat{j}] \times [20\alpha t\hat{i}+5\beta\hat{j}]$

$\vec{L}=m[50\alpha\beta t^{2}\hat{k}-10\alpha\beta(t^{2}-5t)\hat{k}]$

At t = 0, $\vec{L}=\vec{0}$

$50\alpha\beta t^{2}-100\alpha\beta(t^{2}-5t)=0$

t $-$ 2 (t $-$ 5) = 0

t = 10 sec

questions.question_text: A circular disc reaches from top to bottom of an inclined plane of length 'L'. When it slips down the plane, it makes time 't 1 '. When it rolls down the plane, it takes time t 2 . The value of $\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{3}{x}}$ . The value of x will be _______________.
questions.question_html: A circular disc reaches from top to bottom of an inclined plane of length 'L'. When it slips down the plane, it makes time 't1'. When it rolls down the plane, it takes time t2. The value of $\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{3}{x}}$ . The value of x will be _______________.
questions.explanation_text: According to question, a circular disc reaches from top to bottom of an inclined plane of length L. This can be shown as When the disc slips down the inclined plane, it takes time t 1 . Therefore, in this case its acceleration, a 1 = g sin $\theta$ $\because$ s = ut 1 + $\frac{1}{2}$ a 1 t $_{1}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ s = $\frac{1}{2}$ g sin $\theta$ t $_{1}^{2}$ .... (i) And when the disc rolls down the inclined plane, it takes time t 2 . Therefore in this case, its acceleration, $a_{2}=\frac{gsin\theta}{1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}}=\frac{gsin\theta}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{2}{3}gsin\theta$ [ $\because$ for disc, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ ] $\because$ s = ut 2 + $\frac{1}{2}$ a 2 t $_{2}^{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ . $\frac{2}{3}$ g sin $\theta$ t $_{2}^{2}$ .... (ii) On dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$ .... (iii) According to question, value of $\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{3}{x}}$ . Comparing it with Eq. (iii), we get x = 2
questions.explanation_html:
According to question, a circular disc reaches from top to bottom of an inclined plane of length L. This can be shown as


When the disc slips down the inclined plane, it takes time t1. Therefore, in this case its acceleration, a1 = g sin $\theta$

$\because$ s = ut1 + $\frac{1}{2}$ a1t $_{1}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ s = $\frac{1}{2}$ g sin $\theta$ t $_{1}^{2}$ .... (i)

And when the disc rolls down the inclined plane, it takes time t2. Therefore in this case, its acceleration,

$a_{2}=\frac{gsin\theta}{1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}}=\frac{gsin\theta}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{2}{3}gsin\theta$ [ $\because$ for disc, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ ]

$\because$ s = ut2 + $\frac{1}{2}$ a2t $_{2}^{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ . $\frac{2}{3}$ g sin $\theta$ t $_{2}^{2}$ .... (ii)

On dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get

$\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$ .... (iii)

According to question, value of $\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}$ is $\sqrt{\frac{3}{x}}$ .

Comparing it with Eq. (iii), we get x = 2

questions.question_text: Two discs have moments of inertia I 1 and I 2 about their respective axes perpendicular to the plane and passing through the centre. They are rotating with angular speeds, $\omega$ 1 and $\omega$ 2 respectively and are brought into contact face to face with their axes of rotation coaxial. The loss in kinetic energy of the system in the process is given by :
questions.question_html: Two discs have moments of inertia I1 and I2 about their respective axes perpendicular to the plane and passing through the centre. They are rotating with angular speeds, $\omega$ 1 and $\omega$ 2 respectively and are brought into contact face to face with their axes of rotation coaxial. The loss in kinetic energy of the system in the process is given by :
questions.explanation_text: From conservation of angular momentum we get $I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2}=(I_{1}+I_{2})\omega$ $\omega=\frac{I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}}$ $k_{i}=\frac{1}{2}I_{1}\omega_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I_{2}\omega_{2}^{2}$ $k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(I_{1}+I_{2})\omega^{2}$ $k_{i}-k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}[I_{1}\omega_{1}^{2}+I_{2}\omega_{2}^{2}-\frac{(I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2})^{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}}]$ Solving above we get $k_{i}-k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{I_{1}I_{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}})(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
From conservation of angular momentum we get

$I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2}=(I_{1}+I_{2})\omega$

$\omega=\frac{I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}}$

$k_{i}=\frac{1}{2}I_{1}\omega_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I_{2}\omega_{2}^{2}$

$k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(I_{1}+I_{2})\omega^{2}$

$k_{i}-k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}[I_{1}\omega_{1}^{2}+I_{2}\omega_{2}^{2}-\frac{(I_{1}\omega_{1}+I_{2}\omega_{2})^{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}}]$

Solving above we get

$k_{i}-k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{I_{1}I_{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}})(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})^{2}$

questions.question_html: The angular speed of truck wheel is increased from 900 rpm to 2460 rpm in 26 seconds. The number of revolutions by the truck engine during this time is _____________. (Assuming the acceleration to be uniform).
questions.explanation_text: $\omega_{f}=2460 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$ $=82\pi$ $\omega_{i}=\frac{900 \times 2\pi}{60}=30\pi$ $\alpha=\frac{\omega_{f}-\omega_{i}}{t}$ $=\frac{82\pi-30\pi}{26}$ = 2 $\pi$ rad/sec 2 $\theta=\frac{\omega_{f}^{2}-\omega_{i}^{2}}{2\alpha}$ $=\frac{(82\pi+30\pi)(82\pi-30\pi)}{2 \times 2\pi}$ $=\frac{(112 \times 52)\pi^{2}}{4\pi}$ No. of revolution $=\frac{(112 \times 13)\pi}{2\pi}$ = 728
questions.explanation_html:
$\omega_{f}=2460 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$

$=82\pi$

$\omega_{i}=\frac{900 \times 2\pi}{60}=30\pi$

$\alpha=\frac{\omega_{f}-\omega_{i}}{t}$

$=\frac{82\pi-30\pi}{26}$

= 2 $\pi$ rad/sec2

$\theta=\frac{\omega_{f}^{2}-\omega_{i}^{2}}{2\alpha}$

$=\frac{(82\pi+30\pi)(82\pi-30\pi)}{2 \times 2\pi}$

$=\frac{(112 \times 52)\pi^{2}}{4\pi}$

No. of revolution $=\frac{(112 \times 13)\pi}{2\pi}$

= 728

questions.explanation_text: $\alpha=\frac{\tau}{I}=\frac{F.R.}{mR^{2}/2}=\frac{2F}{mR}$ $\alpha=\frac{2 \times 200}{20 \times (0.2)}=10$ rad/s 2 $\omega^{2}=\omega_{0}^{2}+2\alpha\Delta\theta$ $(50)^{2}=0^{2}+2(10)\Delta\theta$ $\Rightarrow \Delta\theta=\frac{2500}{20}$ $\Delta\theta=125$ rad No. of revolution $=\frac{125}{2\pi} \approx 20$ revolution

$\alpha=\frac{\tau}{I}=\frac{F.R.}{mR^{2}/2}=\frac{2F}{mR}$

$\alpha=\frac{2 \times 200}{20 \times (0.2)}=10$ rad/s2

$\Rightarrow \Delta\theta=\frac{2500}{20}$

questions.explanation_text: For translational equilibrium, T + f = mg sin60 $^{\circ}$ ..... (1) For rotational equilibrium, Torque about center of mass should be zero. $\therefore$ $\tau$ com = 0 $\Rightarrow$ f $\times$ R $-$ T $\times$ R = 0 $\Rightarrow$ f = R ..... (2) Putting value of (2) in (1), f + f = mg sin60 $^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow$ f = $\frac{mgsin60^{\circ}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}mg}{4}$ = 0.433 mg $\therefore$ cylinder need minimum 0.433 mg friction force to stay in equilibrium. But here maximum friction force possible, f max = $\mu$ s N = $\mu$ s mg cos60 $^{\circ}$ = 0.4 mg $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}$ = 0.2 mg As maximum possible friction force is less than 0.433 mg. so cylinder will not stay in equilibrium. It will slide on the surface. So friction will be kinetic friction. f k = $\mu$ k N = $\mu$ k mg cos60 $^{\circ}$ = 0.4 mg $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{mg}{5}$
questions.explanation_html:
For translational equilibrium,

T + f = mg sin60 $^{\circ}$ ..... (1)

For rotational equilibrium,

Torque about center of mass should be zero.

$\therefore$ $\tau$ com = 0

$\Rightarrow$ f $\times$ R $-$ T $\times$ R = 0

$\Rightarrow$ f = R ..... (2)

Putting value of (2) in (1),

f + f = mg sin60 $^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow$ f = $\frac{mgsin60^{\circ}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}mg}{4}$ = 0.433 mg

$\therefore$ cylinder need minimum 0.433 mg friction force to stay in equilibrium.

But here maximum friction force possible,

fmax = $\mu$ sN

= $\mu$ smg cos60 $^{\circ}$

= 0.4 mg $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}$

= 0.2 mg

As maximum possible friction force is less than 0.433 mg. so cylinder will not stay in equilibrium. It will slide on the surface. So friction will be kinetic friction.

fk = $\mu$ k N

= $\mu$ k mg cos60 $^{\circ}$

= 0.4 mg $\times$ $\frac{1}{2}$

= $\frac{mg}{5}$

The linear mass density of a thin rod AB of length L varies from A to B as $\lambda(x)=\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})$ , where
x is the distance from A. If M is the mass of the rod then its moment of inertia about an axis passing

questions.question_html:
The linear mass density of a thin rod AB of length L varies from A to B as
$\lambda(x)=\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})$ , where x is the distance from A. If M is the mass of the rod then its moment of inertia about an axis passing through A and perpendicular to the rod is :
questions.explanation_text: dm = $\lambda$ dx = $\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})$ dx Integrating both side, we get $\int_{0}^{M}dm=\int_{0}^{L}\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})dx$ $\Rightarrow$ M = $\lambda_{0}L+\frac{\lambda_{0}L^{2}}{2L}$ = $\frac{3\lambda_{0}L}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda_{0}=\frac{2M}{3L}$ .....(1) Moment of inertia of small part dx is dI = dmx 2 Integrating both side, we get $\int_{0}^{I}dI=\int_{0}^{L}dmx^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ I = $\int_{0}^{L}\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})dxx^{2}$ = $\lambda_{0}\int_{0}^{L}(x^{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{L})dx$ = $\lambda_{0}[\frac{L^{3}}{3}+\frac{L^{3}}{4}]$ = $\frac{7L^{3}\lambda_{0}}{12}$ Here by putting the value of $\lambda$ 0 form (1) I = $\frac{7L^{3}}{12}(\frac{2M}{3L})$ = $\frac{7}{18}ML^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
dm = $\lambda$ dx

= $\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})$ dx

Integrating both side, we get

$\int_{0}^{M}dm=\int_{0}^{L}\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})dx$

$\Rightarrow$ M = $\lambda_{0}L+\frac{\lambda_{0}L^{2}}{2L}$ = $\frac{3\lambda_{0}L}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda_{0}=\frac{2M}{3L}$ .....(1)

Moment of inertia of small part dx is

dI = dmx2

Integrating both side, we get

$\int_{0}^{I}dI=\int_{0}^{L}dmx^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ I = $\int_{0}^{L}\lambda_{0}(1+\frac{x}{L})dxx^{2}$

= $\lambda_{0}\int_{0}^{L}(x^{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{L})dx$

= $\lambda_{0}[\frac{L^{3}}{3}+\frac{L^{3}}{4}]$

= $\frac{7L^{3}\lambda_{0}}{12}$

Here by putting the value of $\lambda$ 0 form (1)

I = $\frac{7L^{3}}{12}(\frac{2M}{3L})$ = $\frac{7}{18}ML^{2}$

questions.question_text:
A wheel is rotating freely with an angular speed $\omega$ on a shaft. The moment of inertia of the
wheel is I and the moment of inertia of the
shaft is negligible. Another wheel of moment of
inertia 3I initially at rest is suddenly coupled to
the same shaft. The resultant fractional loss in
the kinetic energy of the system is :
questions.question_html: A wheel is rotating freely with an angular speed $\omega$ on a shaft. The moment of inertia of the wheel is I and the moment of inertia of the shaft is negligible. Another wheel of moment of inertia 3I initially at rest is suddenly coupled to the same shaft. The resultant fractional loss in the kinetic energy of the system is :
questions.explanation_text: Applying Angular Momentum conservation $I\omega=(I+3I)\omega^{'}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\omega^{'}=\frac{I\omega}{4I}=\frac{\omega}{4}$ $k_{i}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$ $k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(4I)(\omega^{'})^{2}$ $=2I(\frac{\omega}{4})^{2}=\frac{1}{8}I\omega^{2}$ Fractional loss $=\frac{K_{i}-K_{f}}{K_{i}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}-\frac{1}{8}I\omega^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}}$ = $\frac{\frac{3}{8}I\omega^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}}=\frac{3}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
Applying Angular Momentum conservation

$I\omega=(I+3I)\omega^{'}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\omega^{'}=\frac{I\omega}{4I}=\frac{\omega}{4}$

$k_{i}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$

$k_{f}=\frac{1}{2}(4I)(\omega^{'})^{2}$

$=2I(\frac{\omega}{4})^{2}=\frac{1}{8}I\omega^{2}$

Fractional loss $=\frac{K_{i}-K_{f}}{K_{i}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}-\frac{1}{8}I\omega^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}}$

= $\frac{\frac{3}{8}I\omega^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}}=\frac{3}{4}$

I = $M(\frac{R^{2}}{4}+\frac{L^{2}}{12})$ . If such a cylinder is to be made for a given mass of a material, the ratio $\frac{L}{R}$ for it to have minimum possible I is
questions.explanation_text: Given I = $M(\frac{R^{2}}{4}+\frac{L^{2}}{12})$ M = $\rho$ .V = $\rho$ $\pi$ R 2 L $\Rightarrow$ R 2 = $\frac{M}{\rho\pi L}$ $\therefore$ I = $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi L}+\frac{L^{2}}{12})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dI}{dL}$ = $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi}(-\frac{1}{L^{2}})-\frac{2L}{12})$ For minimum I, $\frac{dI}{dL}=0$ $\therefore$ $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi}(-\frac{1}{L^{2}})-\frac{2L}{12})$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{M^{2}}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{2LM}{12}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{M}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{L}{6}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\rho\pi R^{2}L}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{L}{6}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{R^{2}}{L^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{R}{L}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{L}{R}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given I = $M(\frac{R^{2}}{4}+\frac{L^{2}}{12})$

M = $\rho$ .V = $\rho$ $\pi$ R2L

$\Rightarrow$ R2 = $\frac{M}{\rho\pi L}$

$\therefore$ I = $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi L}+\frac{L^{2}}{12})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dI}{dL}$ = $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi}(-\frac{1}{L^{2}})-\frac{2L}{12})$

For minimum I, $\frac{dI}{dL}=0$

$\therefore$ $M(\frac{M}{4\rho\pi}(-\frac{1}{L^{2}})-\frac{2L}{12})$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{M^{2}}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{2LM}{12}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{M}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{L}{6}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\rho\pi R^{2}L}{4\rho\pi L^{2}}=\frac{L}{6}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{R^{2}}{L^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{R}{L}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{L}{R}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$

By conservation of energy :

Loss in energy = Gain in enrgy

m1gh = m2gh + $\frac{1}{2}$ m1V2 + $\frac{1}{2}$ m2V2 + $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ (m1 – m2)gh = $\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}[(m_{1}+m_{2})R^{2}+I]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\omega$ = $[\frac{2(m_{1}-m_{2})gℎ}{(m_{1}+m_{2})R^{2}+I}]^{\frac{1}{2}}$

questions.question_html: Two uniform circular discs are rotating independently in the same direction around their common axis passing through their centres. = $\frac{20}{3}J$

questions.explanation_text: $F_{v}=mg$ $F_{H}=m\omega^{2}\frac{l}{2}sin\theta$ $\therefore$ $\tau_{net}aboutCOM=F_{v}.\frac{l}{2}sin\theta-F_{H}\frac{l}{2}cos\theta$ $=\frac{ml^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}sin\theta cos\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $mg\frac{l}{2}sin\theta-m\omega^{2}\frac{l}{2}sin\theta\frac{l}{2}cos\theta=\frac{ml^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}sin\theta cos\theta$ $\Rightarrow \frac{gl}{2}-\frac{\omega^{2}l^{2}}{4}cos\theta=\frac{l^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}cos\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{gl}{2}=\omega^{2}l^{2}cos\theta(\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{4})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{gl}{2}=\frac{\omega^{2}l^{2}cos\theta}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $cos\theta=\frac{3g}{2\omega^{2}l}$
questions.explanation_html:
$F_{v}=mg$

$F_{H}=m\omega^{2}\frac{l}{2}sin\theta$

$\therefore$ $\tau_{net}aboutCOM=F_{v}.\frac{l}{2}sin\theta-F_{H}\frac{l}{2}cos\theta$

$=\frac{ml^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}sin\theta cos\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $mg\frac{l}{2}sin\theta-m\omega^{2}\frac{l}{2}sin\theta\frac{l}{2}cos\theta=\frac{ml^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}sin\theta cos\theta$

$\Rightarrow \frac{gl}{2}-\frac{\omega^{2}l^{2}}{4}cos\theta=\frac{l^{2}}{12}\omega^{2}cos\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{gl}{2}=\omega^{2}l^{2}cos\theta(\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{4})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{gl}{2}=\frac{\omega^{2}l^{2}cos\theta}{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $cos\theta=\frac{3g}{2\omega^{2}l}$

questions.explanation_text: $I_{f}\omega_{f}=I_{i}\omega_{i}$ $I_{i}=\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$ $I_{f}=\frac{MR^{2}}{2}+\frac{M(R/2)^{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{5}{4}.\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$ $[\frac{MR^{2}}{2}+\frac{M}{2}(\frac{R}{2})^{2}]\omega^{'}=(\frac{MR^{2}}{2}).\omega$ $\Rightarrow$ $[\frac{MR^{2}}{2}.(\frac{5}{4})]\omega^{'}=\frac{MR^{2}}{2}\omega$ $\omega=\frac{4}{5}\omega$ loss of K.E. = $\frac{Loss}{K_{i}} \times 100$ = $\frac{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{5}{4}I)(\frac{4}{5}\omega)^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}}$ $\times$ 100 = $\frac{\omega^{2}-\frac{16}{25}\omega^{2}(\frac{5}{4})}{\omega^{2}}$ $\times$ 100 = $(1-\frac{80}{100}) \times 100$ = 20%

questions.question_html: The following bodies are made to roll up (without slipping) the same inclined plane from a horizontal plane. : (i) a ring of radius R, (ii) a solid cylinder of radius R/2 and (iii) a solid sphere of radius R/4 . If in each case, the speed of the centre of mass at the bottom of the incline is same, the ratio of the maximum heights they climb is :
questions.explanation_text: Total kinetic energy of a rolling body is given as $E_{\text{total}}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}]$ where, $K$ is the radius of gyration. Using conservation law of energy, $\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}]=mgℎ \\ \\ \text{or}ℎ=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}] \end{aligned}$ For ring, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$ $\Rightarrow ℎ_{1}=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+1]=\frac{2v^{2}}{2g}=\frac{v^{2}}{g}$ For solid cylinder, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{(R/2\sqrt{2})^{2}}{(R/2)^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{R^{2}}{8} \times \frac{4}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ \Rightarrow ℎ_{2} & =\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{1}{2}]=\frac{3v^{2}}{4g} \end{aligned}$ For solid sphere, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}$ $\Rightarrow ℎ_{3}=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{2}{5}]=\frac{7v^{2}}{10g}$ So,the ratio of $ℎ_{1},ℎ_{2}$ and $ℎ_{3}$ is $\begin{aligned} ℎ_{1}:ℎ_{2}:ℎ_{3} & =\frac{v^{2}}{g}:\frac{3v^{2}}{4g}:\frac{7}{10}\frac{v^{2}}{g} \\ \\ & =1:\frac{3}{4}:\frac{7}{10}=20:15:14 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Total kinetic energy of a rolling body is given as

$E_{\text{total}}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}]$

where, $K$ is the radius of gyration.

Using conservation law of energy,

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}]=mgℎ \\ \\ \text{or}ℎ=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}] \end{aligned}$

For ring, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$

$\Rightarrow ℎ_{1}=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+1]=\frac{2v^{2}}{2g}=\frac{v^{2}}{g}$

For solid cylinder, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{(R/2\sqrt{2})^{2}}{(R/2)^{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{R^{2}}{8} \times \frac{4}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ \Rightarrow ℎ_{2} & =\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{1}{2}]=\frac{3v^{2}}{4g} \end{aligned}$

For solid sphere, $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}$

$\Rightarrow ℎ_{3}=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}[1+\frac{2}{5}]=\frac{7v^{2}}{10g}$

So,the ratio of $ℎ_{1},ℎ_{2}$ and $ℎ_{3}$ is

$\begin{aligned} ℎ_{1}:ℎ_{2}:ℎ_{3} & =\frac{v^{2}}{g}:\frac{3v^{2}}{4g}:\frac{7}{10}\frac{v^{2}}{g} \\ \\ & =1:\frac{3}{4}:\frac{7}{10}=20:15:14 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Angular momentum conservation MV 0 L = MV 1 (L – $\ell$ ) $V_{1}=V_{0}(\frac{L}{L-\ell})$ $w_{g}+w_{p}=\Delta KE$ $-mg\ell+w_{p}=\frac{1}{2}m(V_{1}^{2}-V_{0}^{2})$ $w_{p}=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{2}-1)$ $=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((1-\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{-2}-1)$ Now $\ell≪L$ By, Binomial approximation $=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((1+\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{-2}-1)$ $=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}(\frac{2\ell}{L})$ $w_{p}=mg\ell+mV_{0}^{2}\frac{\ell}{L}$ Here, V 0 = maximum velocity = $\omega \times A=(\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}})(\theta_{0}L)$ So, $w_{p}=mg\ell+m(\theta_{0}\sqrt{gL})^{2}\frac{\ell}{L}$ = $mg\ell(1+\theta_{0}^{2})$
questions.explanation_html:
Angular momentum conservation
MV0L = MV1(L – $\ell$ )

$V_{1}=V_{0}(\frac{L}{L-\ell})$

$w_{g}+w_{p}=\Delta KE$

$-mg\ell+w_{p}=\frac{1}{2}m(V_{1}^{2}-V_{0}^{2})$

$w_{p}=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{2}-1)$

$=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((1-\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{-2}-1)$

Now $\ell≪L$

By, Binomial approximation

$=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}((1+\frac{L}{L-\ell})^{-2}-1)$

$=mg\ell+\frac{1}{2}mV_{0}^{2}(\frac{2\ell}{L})$

$w_{p}=mg\ell+mV_{0}^{2}\frac{\ell}{L}$

Here, V0 = maximum velocity = $\omega \times A=(\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}})(\theta_{0}L)$

So, $w_{p}=mg\ell+m(\theta_{0}\sqrt{gL})^{2}\frac{\ell}{L}$

= $mg\ell(1+\theta_{0}^{2})$

questions.question_html: A thin disc of mass M and radius R has mass per unit area $\sigma$ (r) = kr2 where r is the distance from its centre. Its moment of inertia about an axis going through its centre of mass and perpendicular to its plane is :
questions.explanation_text: $I_{Disc}=\int_{0}^{R}(dm)r^{2} \Rightarrow I_{Disc}=\int_{0}^{R}(\sigma 2\pi rdr)r^{2}$ $I_{Disc}=\int_{0}^{R}(kr^{2}2\pi rdr)r^{2}$ Mass of Disc $I_{Disc}=2\pi k\int_{0}^{R}r^{2}drM=\int_{0}^{R}2\pi rdrkr^{2}$ $I_{Disc}=2\pi k(\frac{r^{6}}{6})_{0}^{R}M=2\pi k\int_{0}^{R}r^{3}dr$ $I_{Disc}=2\pi k\frac{R^{6}}{6}M=2\pi k\frac{r^{4}}{4}|_{0}^{R}$ $I_{Disc}=\frac{\pi kR^{6}}{3}=(\frac{\pi kR^{4}}{2})\frac{R^{2}2}{3}M=2\pi k\frac{r^{4}}{4}|_{0}^{R}$ $I_{Disc}=\frac{M2R^{2}}{3};I_{Disc}=\frac{2}{3}MR^{2}$

questions.question_text: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere, about an axis parallel to its diameter and at a distance of x from it, is 'I(x)'. Which one of the graphs represents the variation of I(x) with x correctly ?
questions.question_html: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere, about an axis parallel to its diameter and at a distance of x from it, is 'I(x)'. Which one of the graphs represents the variation of I(x) with x correctly ?

options.label: A
B
C
D

questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option C . Here's why : The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about an axis passing through its center is given by : $I_{0}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ Where : $I_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the center $M$ is the mass of the sphere $R$ is the radius of the sphere Now, using the parallel axis theorem, we can find the moment of inertia about an axis parallel to the diameter and at a distance of 'x' from it : $I(x)=I_{0}+Mx^{2}$ Substituting the value of $I_{0}$ : $I(x)=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}+Mx^{2}$ This equation represents a parabola, where : The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is positive (M), indicating an upward-opening parabola. The y-intercept (the value of $I(x)$ when $x=0$ ) is $\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ , which is a positive constant. Therefore, the graph of $I(x)$ vs. $x$ should be an upward-opening parabola, and Option C accurately represents this.
questions.explanation_html:
The correct answer is Option C. Here's why :

The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about an axis passing through its center is given by :

$I_{0}=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$

Where :

  • $I_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the center
  • $M$ is the mass of the sphere
  • $R$ is the radius of the sphere

Now, using the parallel axis theorem, we can find the moment of inertia about an axis parallel to the diameter and at a distance of 'x' from it :

$I(x)=I_{0}+Mx^{2}$

Substituting the value of $I_{0}$ :

$I(x)=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}+Mx^{2}$

This equation represents a parabola, where :

  • The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is positive (M), indicating an upward-opening parabola.
  • The y-intercept (the value of $I(x)$ when $x=0$ ) is $\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$ , which is a positive constant.

Therefore, the graph of $I(x)$ vs. $x$ should be an upward-opening parabola, and Option C accurately represents this.

questions.question_html: A slab is subjected to two forces $\vec{F_{1}}$ and $\vec{F_{2}}$ of same magnitude F as shown in the figure. Force $\vec{F_{2}}$ is in XY-plane while force $\vec{F_{1}}$ acts along z = axis at the point $(2\vec{i}+3\vec{j}).$ . The moment of these forces about point O will be :
questions.explanation_text: To determine the moment of the forces about point O, we need to calculate the moments of each force and then combine them vectorially. First, consider force $\vec{F_{1}}$ . This force acts along the z-axis at the point $(2\vec{i}+3\vec{j})$ . The position vector of the point of application of $\vec{F_{1}}$ relative to the origin O is: $\vec{r_{1}}=2\vec{i}+3\vec{j}$ Since $\vec{F_{1}}$ acts along the z-axis, we can express it as: $\vec{F_{1}}=F\vec{k}$ The moment of force $\vec{F_{1}}$ about point O is given by the cross product: $\vec{M_{1}}=\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{F_{1}}$ Substitute the values: $\vec{M_{1}}=(2\vec{i}+3\vec{j}) \times F\vec{k}$ Compute the cross product: $\vec{M_{1}}=2F(\vec{i} \times \vec{k})+3F(\vec{j} \times \vec{k})$ $\vec{M_{1}}=2F(-\vec{j})+3F\vec{i}$ $\vec{M_{1}}=-2F\vec{j}+3F\vec{i}$ So, the moment due to force $\vec{F_{1}}$ is: $\vec{M_{1}}=3F\vec{i}-2F\vec{j}$ Torque for F 2 force $\vec{F}_{2}$ = $\frac{F}{2}(-\hat{i})+\frac{F\sqrt{3}}{2}(-\hat{j})$ $\vec{r}_{1}=0\hat{i}+6\hat{j}$ $\vec{\tau}_{_{F_{2}}}=\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{F_{1}}=3F\hat{k}$ $\vec{\tau}_{net}=\vec{\tau}_{F_{1}}+\vec{\tau}_{f_{2}}$ $=3F\hat{i}+2F(-\hat{j})+3F(\hat{k})$
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the moment of the forces about point O, we need to calculate the moments of each force and then combine them vectorially.

First, consider force $\vec{F_{1}}$ . This force acts along the z-axis at the point $(2\vec{i}+3\vec{j})$ .

The position vector of the point of application of $\vec{F_{1}}$ relative to the origin O is:

$\vec{r_{1}}=2\vec{i}+3\vec{j}$

Since $\vec{F_{1}}$ acts along the z-axis, we can express it as:

$\vec{F_{1}}=F\vec{k}$

The moment of force $\vec{F_{1}}$ about point O is given by the cross product:

$\vec{M_{1}}=\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{F_{1}}$

Substitute the values:

$\vec{M_{1}}=(2\vec{i}+3\vec{j}) \times F\vec{k}$

Compute the cross product:

$\vec{M_{1}}=2F(\vec{i} \times \vec{k})+3F(\vec{j} \times \vec{k})$ $\vec{M_{1}}=2F(-\vec{j})+3F\vec{i}$ $\vec{M_{1}}=-2F\vec{j}+3F\vec{i}$

So, the moment due to force $\vec{F_{1}}$ is:

$\vec{M_{1}}=3F\vec{i}-2F\vec{j}$

Torque for F2 force

$\vec{F}_{2}$ = $\frac{F}{2}(-\hat{i})+\frac{F\sqrt{3}}{2}(-\hat{j})$

$\vec{r}_{1}=0\hat{i}+6\hat{j}$

$\vec{\tau}_{_{F_{2}}}=\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{F_{1}}=3F\hat{k}$

$\vec{\tau}_{net}=\vec{\tau}_{F_{1}}+\vec{\tau}_{f_{2}}$

$=3F\hat{i}+2F(-\hat{j})+3F(\hat{k})$

From a uniform circular disc of radius R and mass 9M, a small disc

questions.question_html: From a uniform circular disc of radius R and mass 9M, a small disc of radius R/3 is removed as shown in the figure. The moment of inertia of the remaining disc about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the disc and passing through centre of disc is :
questions.explanation_text: Given that for a uniform circular disc the radius is R and mass 9M $\therefore$ The area of uniform circular disc = $\pi R^{2}$ The radius of removed portion = $\frac{R}{3}$ $\therefore$ The area of removed portion = $\frac{\pi R^{2}}{9}$ So the mass of the removed portion = $\frac{9M}{9}$ = M If the moment of inertia of removed disc about the center of the circular disc of radius R is I 1 then I 1 = $\frac{1}{2}M(\frac{R}{3})^{2}+M(\frac{2R}{3})^{2}$ = $\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$ Moment of inertia of the whole disc, I 2 = $\frac{9MR^{2}}{2}$ Moment of inertia of the remaining disc, I = I 2 - I 1 $\therefore$ I = $\frac{9MR^{2}}{2}-\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$ = $4MR^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that for a uniform circular disc the radius is R and mass 9M

$\therefore$ The area of uniform circular disc = $\pi R^{2}$

The radius of removed portion = $\frac{R}{3}$

$\therefore$ The area of removed portion = $\frac{\pi R^{2}}{9}$

So the mass of the removed portion = $\frac{9M}{9}$ = M

If the moment of inertia of removed disc about the center of the circular disc of radius R is I1 then

I1 = $\frac{1}{2}M(\frac{R}{3})^{2}+M(\frac{2R}{3})^{2}$ = $\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$

Moment of inertia of the whole disc, I2 = $\frac{9MR^{2}}{2}$

Moment of inertia of the remaining disc, I = I2 - I1

$\therefore$ I = $\frac{9MR^{2}}{2}-\frac{MR^{2}}{2}$ = $4MR^{2}$

questions.question_html: A thin uniform bar of length $L$ and mass $8$ m lies on a smooth horizontal table. questions.explanation_text: Centre of mass after the collision will be at O. Therefore, $2m\frac{L}{6}=m\frac{L}{3}$ Now, using conservation of angular momentum, we get $2m\frac{L}{6} \times v+m\frac{L}{3} \times 2v=I\omega$ Therefore, $2m\frac{L}{6} \times v+m\frac{L}{3} \times 2v=[8m\frac{L^{2}}{12}+2m(\frac{L}{6})^{2}+m(\frac{L}{3})^{2}]\omega$ $\Rightarrow (\frac{L}{6}+\frac{L}{3})2mv=[8m\frac{L^{2}}{12}+\frac{2mL^{2}}{36}+\frac{mL^{2}}{9}]\omega$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3L}{6} \times 2mV=\frac{5}{6}mL^{2}\omega$ $\Rightarrow Lmv=\frac{5}{6}mL^{2}\omega \Rightarrow \omega=\frac{6Lmv}{5mL^{2}} \Rightarrow \omega=\frac{6}{5}\frac{v}{L}$
questions.explanation_html:
Centre of mass after the collision will be at O. Therefore,

$2m\frac{L}{6}=m\frac{L}{3}$

Now, using conservation of angular momentum, we get

$2m\frac{L}{6} \times v+m\frac{L}{3} \times 2v=I\omega$

Therefore,

$2m\frac{L}{6} \times v+m\frac{L}{3} \times 2v=[8m\frac{L^{2}}{12}+2m(\frac{L}{6})^{2}+m(\frac{L}{3})^{2}]\omega$

$\Rightarrow (\frac{L}{6}+\frac{L}{3})2mv=[8m\frac{L^{2}}{12}+\frac{2mL^{2}}{36}+\frac{mL^{2}}{9}]\omega$

$\Rightarrow \frac{3L}{6} \times 2mV=\frac{5}{6}mL^{2}\omega$

$\Rightarrow Lmv=\frac{5}{6}mL^{2}\omega \Rightarrow \omega=\frac{6Lmv}{5mL^{2}} \Rightarrow \omega=\frac{6}{5}\frac{v}{L}$

questions.question_html: Seven identical circular planar disks, each of mass M and radius R are welded symmetrically as shown. The moment of inertia of the arrangement about the axis normal to the plane and passing through the point P is :
questions.explanation_text: Moment of inertia of any disc form its center perpendicular to the plane of disc = $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ Moment of inertia of any one of the outer disc about an axis passing through point O and perpendicular to the plane $I_{1}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+M(2R)^{2}$ = $\frac{9}{2}MR^{2}$ Moment of inertia of the entire system about point O $I_{o}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+6I_{1}$ = $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+6 \times \frac{9}{2}MR^{2}$ = $\frac{55}{2}MR^{2}$ By symmetry, point $O$ is center of mass of the complete configuration. The point $P$ is located at a distance $d_{p}=3R$ from the center of mass $O$ . The parallel axis theorem gives moment of inertia of the configuration about a normal axis through $P$ as $I_{P}=I_{O}+7M(3R)^{2}$ = $\frac{55}{2}MR^{2}+63MR^{2}$ = $\frac{181}{2}MR^{2}$

Moment of inertia of any disc form its center perpendicular to the plane of disc = $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$

Moment of inertia of any one of the outer disc about an axis passing through point O and perpendicular to the plane

Moment of inertia of the entire system about point O

$I_{o}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+6I_{1}$

= $\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+6 \times \frac{9}{2}MR^{2}$

= $\frac{55}{2}MR^{2}$

By symmetry, point $O$ is center of mass of the complete configuration. The point $P$ is located at a distance $d_{p}=3R$ from the center of mass $O$ . The parallel axis theorem gives moment of inertia of the configuration about a normal axis through $P$ as

$I_{P}=I_{O}+7M(3R)^{2}$

= $\frac{55}{2}MR^{2}+63MR^{2}$

= $\frac{181}{2}MR^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ m = $(\frac{m\ell}{2})\frac{1}{x}-M$

Comparing this straight line equation, y = mx + c

questions.question_text:
The moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $l$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is $I$ .
What is the ratio $\frac{l}{R}$ such that the moment of inertia is minimum?
questions.question_html: The moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $l$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is $I$ . What is the ratio $\frac{l}{R}$ such that the moment of inertia is minimum?
questions.explanation_text: The volume of the cylinder V = $\pi R^{2}l$ $\therefore$ $R^{2}=\frac{V}{\pi l}$ We know, moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $l$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is, $I=\frac{Ml^{2}}{12}+\frac{MR^{2}}{4}$ [ Putting $R^{2}=\frac{V}{\pi l}$ in this equation] $\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{Ml^{2}}{12}+\frac{MV}{4\pi l}$ Here $I$ is a function of $l$ as M and V are constant. $I$ will be maximum or minimum when $\frac{dI}{dl}$ = 0. $\Rightarrow \frac{Ml}{6}-\frac{MV}{4\pi l^{2}}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{Ml}{6}=\frac{MV}{4\pi l^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{l}{6}=\frac{\pi R^{2}l}{4\pi l^{2}}$ [ as $V=\pi R^{2}l$ ] $\Rightarrow \frac{R^{2}}{l^{2}}=\frac{4}{6}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{l}{R}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
The volume of the cylinder V = $\pi R^{2}l$

$\therefore$ $R^{2}=\frac{V}{\pi l}$

We know, moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $l$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is,

$I=\frac{Ml^{2}}{12}+\frac{MR^{2}}{4}$

[ Putting $R^{2}=\frac{V}{\pi l}$ in this equation]

$\Rightarrow$ $I=\frac{Ml^{2}}{12}+\frac{MV}{4\pi l}$

Here $I$ is a function of $l$ as M and V are constant.

$I$ will be maximum or minimum when $\frac{dI}{dl}$ = 0.

$\Rightarrow \frac{Ml}{6}-\frac{MV}{4\pi l^{2}}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{Ml}{6}=\frac{MV}{4\pi l^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{l}{6}=\frac{\pi R^{2}l}{4\pi l^{2}}$ [ as $V=\pi R^{2}l$ ]

$\Rightarrow \frac{R^{2}}{l^{2}}=\frac{4}{6}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{l}{R}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$

$\vec{L}=m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$

$\vec{L}=m[(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}) \times v(-\hat{j})]$

For the particle moving from $A \rightarrow B$ , we have

$\vec{L}=m[(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}) \times v\hat{i}]$

$=\frac{mvR}{\sqrt{2}}(-\hat{k})$

For the particle moving from $C \rightarrow D$ , we have

$\vec{L}=mv \times$ ( $\perp$ distance) $\times$ $(\hat{k})$

$=mv(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}+a)(\hat{k})$

For the particle moving from $B \rightarrow C$ , we get

$\vec{L}=mv \times$ ( $\perp$ distance) $\times$ $(\hat{k})$

$=mv(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}+a)(\hat{k})$

questions.question_text: From a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ a cube of maximum possible volume is cut. Moment of inertia of cube about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to one of its face is:
questions.question_html: From a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ a cube of maximum possible volume is cut. Moment of inertia of cube about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to one of its face is:
questions.explanation_text: 1. Determine the side length of the cube: The cube with the maximum possible volume that can be cut from the sphere will have its diagonal equal to the diameter of the sphere. Let the side length of the cube be 'a'. Using Pythagoras in 3D, we have: $a^{2}+a^{2}+a^{2}=(2R)^{2}$ $3a^{2}=4R^{2}$ $a=\sqrt{\frac{4R^{2}}{3}}=\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}}$ 2. Calculate the mass of the cube: The volume of the cube is $V=a^{3}=(\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}})^{3}=\frac{8R^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}}$ The density of the sphere (and hence the cube) is $\rho=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}$ The mass of the cube is $m=\rho V=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} \cdot \frac{8R^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2M}{\sqrt{3}\pi}$ 3. Find the moment of inertia of the cube: The moment of inertia of a cube about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to one of its faces is given by: $I=\frac{1}{6}ma^{2}$ Substituting the values we found: $I=\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{2M}{\sqrt{3}\pi} \cdot (\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}})^{2}$ $I=\frac{4MR^{2}}{9\sqrt{3}\pi}$ Therefore, the correct answer is Option A: $\frac{4MR^{2}}{9\sqrt{3\pi}}$
questions.explanation_html:
1. Determine the side length of the cube:

The cube with the maximum possible volume that can be cut from the sphere will have its diagonal equal to the diameter of the sphere. Let the side length of the cube be 'a'. Using Pythagoras in 3D, we have:

$a^{2}+a^{2}+a^{2}=(2R)^{2}$

$3a^{2}=4R^{2}$

$a=\sqrt{\frac{4R^{2}}{3}}=\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}}$

2. Calculate the mass of the cube:

The volume of the cube is $V=a^{3}=(\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}})^{3}=\frac{8R^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}}$

The density of the sphere (and hence the cube) is $\rho=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}$

The mass of the cube is $m=\rho V=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} \cdot \frac{8R^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2M}{\sqrt{3}\pi}$

3. Find the moment of inertia of the cube:

The moment of inertia of a cube about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to one of its faces is given by:

$I=\frac{1}{6}ma^{2}$

Substituting the values we found:

$I=\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{2M}{\sqrt{3}\pi} \cdot (\frac{2R}{\sqrt{3}})^{2}$

$I=\frac{4MR^{2}}{9\sqrt{3}\pi}$

Therefore, the correct answer is Option A: $\frac{4MR^{2}}{9\sqrt{3\pi}}$

questions.explanation_text: Given $F=20t-5t^{2}$ , R = 2 m and $I$ = 10 kg m 2 Torque applied on pulley $\tau=FR$ $\therefore$ $\alpha=\frac{FR}{I}$ [ as $\tau=I\alpha$ ] $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=\frac{(20t-5t^{2}) \times 2}{10}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=4t-t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{d\omega}{dt}=4t-t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{\omega}d\omega=\int_{0}^{t}(4t-t^{2})dt$ $\Rightarrow \omega=2t^{2}-\frac{r^{3}}{3}$ ( At $t=0,6s$ $\omega=0$ ) $\omega=\frac{d\theta}{dt}=2t^{2}-\frac{t^{3}}{3}$ $\int_{0}^{\theta}d\theta=\int_{0}^{6}(2t^{2}-\frac{r^{3}}{3})dt$ $\Rightarrow \theta=36rad \Rightarrow n=\frac{36}{2\pi}<6$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $F=20t-5t^{2}$ , R = 2 m and $I$ = 10 kg m2

Torque applied on pulley $\tau=FR$

$\therefore$ $\alpha=\frac{FR}{I}$ [ as $\tau=I\alpha$ ]

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=\frac{(20t-5t^{2}) \times 2}{10}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha=4t-t^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{d\omega}{dt}=4t-t^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{\omega}d\omega=\int_{0}^{t}(4t-t^{2})dt$

$\Rightarrow \omega=2t^{2}-\frac{r^{3}}{3}$

( At $t=0,6s$ $\omega=0$ )

$\omega=\frac{d\theta}{dt}=2t^{2}-\frac{t^{3}}{3}$

$\int_{0}^{\theta}d\theta=\int_{0}^{6}(2t^{2}-\frac{r^{3}}{3})dt$

$\Rightarrow \theta=36rad \Rightarrow n=\frac{36}{2\pi}<6$

questions.question_html:
A small particle of mass $m$ is projected at an angle $\theta$ with the $x$ -axis with an initial velocity $v_{0}$ in the $x$ - $y$ plane as shown in the figure. At a time $t<\frac{v_{0}sin\theta}{g},$ the angular momentum of the particle is ................,



where $\hat{i},\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are unit vectors along $x,y$ and $z$ -axis respectively.
questions.explanation_text: Position vector of the particle from the original at any time t is $\vec{r}=v_{0}tcos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}tsin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j}$ As Velocity vector, $\vec{v}=\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{v}=\frac{d}{dt}(v_{0}tcos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}tsin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j})$ $=v_{0}cos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta-gt)\hat{j}$ Angular momentum of the particle about the origin is $\vec{L}=m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{L}=m[v_{0}cos\theta t\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta t-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j}] \\ & \times [v_{0}cos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta-gt)\hat{j}] \end{aligned}$ $=mv_{0}cos\theta t[-\frac{1}{2}gt]\hat{k}$ $=-\frac{1}{2}mgv_{0}t^{2}cos\theta\hat{k}$
questions.explanation_html:
Position vector of the particle from the original at any time t is

$\vec{r}=v_{0}tcos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}tsin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j}$

As Velocity vector, $\vec{v}=\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{v}=\frac{d}{dt}(v_{0}tcos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}tsin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j})$

$=v_{0}cos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta-gt)\hat{j}$

Angular momentum of the particle about the origin is

$\vec{L}=m(\vec{r} \times \vec{v})$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{L}=m[v_{0}cos\theta t\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta t-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2})\hat{j}] \\ & \times [v_{0}cos\theta\hat{i}+(v_{0}sin\theta-gt)\hat{j}] \end{aligned}$

$=mv_{0}cos\theta t[-\frac{1}{2}gt]\hat{k}$

$=-\frac{1}{2}mgv_{0}t^{2}cos\theta\hat{k}$

questions.question_html: A particle performing uniform circular motion has angular frequency is doubled & its kinetic energy halved, then the new angular momentum is
questions.explanation_text: We know Rotational Kinetic Energy $=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2},$ Angular Momentum $L=I\omega \Rightarrow I=\frac{L}{\omega}$ $\therefore$ Initial $K.E.=\frac{1}{2}\frac{L}{\omega} \times \omega^{2}=\frac{1}{2}L\omega$ Final $K.E^{'}$ = $\frac{K.E}{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}L^{'} \times 2\omega$ $\therefore$ $\frac{K.E}{K.E^{'}}=\frac{L \times \omega}{L^{'} \times \omega^{'}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{K.E}{\frac{K.E}{2}}=\frac{L \times \omega}{L^{'} \times 2\omega}$ $\therefore$ $L^{'}=\frac{L}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
We know Rotational Kinetic Energy $=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2},$

Angular Momentum $L=I\omega \Rightarrow I=\frac{L}{\omega}$

$\therefore$ Initial $K.E.=\frac{1}{2}\frac{L}{\omega} \times \omega^{2}=\frac{1}{2}L\omega$

Final $K.E^{'}$ = $\frac{K.E}{2}$ = $\frac{1}{2}L^{'} \times 2\omega$

$\therefore$ $\frac{K.E}{K.E^{'}}=\frac{L \times \omega}{L^{'} \times \omega^{'}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{K.E}{\frac{K.E}{2}}=\frac{L \times \omega}{L^{'} \times 2\omega}$

$\therefore$ $L^{'}=\frac{L}{4}$

questions.question_text: A circular disc $X$ of radius $R$ is made from an iron plate of thickness $t,$ and another disc $Y$ of radius $4$ $R$ is made from an iron plate of thickness $\frac{t}{4}.$ Then the relation between the moment of inertia $I_{X}$ and $I_{Y}$ is
questions.question_html: A circular disc $X$ of radius $R$ is made from an iron plate of thickness $t,$ and another disc $Y$ of radius $4$ $R$ is made from an iron plate of thickness $\frac{t}{4}.$ Then the relation between the moment of inertia $I_{X}$ and $I_{Y}$ is
questions.explanation_text: We know that density $(d)=\frac{mass(M)}{volume(V)}$ $\therefore$ Mass of disc $M=d \times V=d \times (\pi R^{2} \times t).$ The moment of inertia of any disc is $I=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ $\therefore$ $I=\frac{1}{2}(d \times \pi R^{2} \times t)R^{2}=\frac{\pi d}{2}t \times R^{4}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{I_{X}}{I_{Y}}=\frac{t_{X}R_{X}^{4}}{t_{Y}R_{Y}^{4}}$ $=\frac{t \times R^{4}}{\frac{t}{4} \times (4R)^{4}}$ $=\frac{1}{64}$
questions.explanation_html:
We know that density $(d)=\frac{mass(M)}{volume(V)}$

$\therefore$ Mass of disc $M=d \times V=d \times (\pi R^{2} \times t).$

The moment of inertia of any disc is $I=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$

$\therefore$ $I=\frac{1}{2}(d \times \pi R^{2} \times t)R^{2}=\frac{\pi d}{2}t \times R^{4}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{I_{X}}{I_{Y}}=\frac{t_{X}R_{X}^{4}}{t_{Y}R_{Y}^{4}}$

$=\frac{t \times R^{4}}{\frac{t}{4} \times (4R)^{4}}$

$=\frac{1}{64}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{F}$ be the force acting on a particle having position vector $\vec{r},$ and $\vec{\tau}$ be the torque of this force about the origin. Then
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{F}$ be the force acting on a particle having position vector $\vec{r},$ and $\vec{\tau}$ be the torque of this force about the origin. Then
questions.explanation_text: As we know $\vec{\tau}=\vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ So the angle between $\vec{\tau}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $90^{\circ}$ and the angle between $\vec{t}$ and $\vec{F}$ is also $90^{\circ}.$ We also know that the dot product of two vectors which have an angle of $90^{\circ}$ between them is zero. $\therefore$ $\vec{r.}\vec{\tau}=0$ and $\vec{F.}\vec{\tau}=0$ Therefore $(d)$ is the correct option.
questions.explanation_html:
As we know $\vec{\tau}=\vec{r} \times \vec{F}$

So the angle between $\vec{\tau}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $90^{\circ}$ and the angle between $\vec{t}$ and $\vec{F}$ is also $90^{\circ}.$

We also know that the dot product of two vectors which have an angle of $90^{\circ}$ between them is zero.

$\therefore$ $\vec{r.}\vec{\tau}=0$ and $\vec{F.}\vec{\tau}=0$

Therefore $(d)$ is the correct option.

Then by perpendicular axis theorem $I_{X}+I_{Y}=I_{Z}$ $\Rightarrow 2I_{X}=MR^{2}$ $[$ as $I_{X}-I_{Y}$ (by symmetry) and $I_{Z}=MR^{2}$ $]$ $\therefore$ $I_{X}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Moment of Inertia of a circular wire about an axis $nn^{'}$ passing through the centre of the circle and perpendicular to the plane of the circle $=MR^{2}$

As shown in the figure, $X$ -axis and $Y$ -axis lies in the plane of the ring. Then by perpendicular axis theorem

$I_{X}+I_{Y}=I_{Z}$

$\Rightarrow 2I_{X}=MR^{2}$ $[$ as $I_{X}-I_{Y}$ (by symmetry) and $I_{Z}=MR^{2}$ $]$

$\therefore$ $I_{X}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$
